NEURAL NETWORKS AT WORK
Six live models · every number computed in your browser
One idea, six jobs

Same machinery.
Six different jobs.

Weighted sums, an activation, a loss and gradient descent. The same few building blocks approve mortgages, tell cats from dogs, read handwriting, value houses and write text. Each chapter below runs a real, trained network and walks through its calculation step by step.

01Credit scoring 02Cat or dog 03Handwritten digits 04House valuation 05Next word 06Complete a sentence
Chapter 01 · Classification · numbers in, yes or no out

Credit scoring

Six facts about a mortgage applicant go in. Out comes a probability of repayment, and a cut-off turns it into approve or reject. Explain mode walks through a full training step, backpropagation included; Train runs thousands of them.

Chapter 02 · Image classification · pixels in, a label out

Cat or dog?

The network receives 784 pixel brightnesses. Instead of weighing every pixel separately, it slides small learned filters across the image to find local patterns such as pointed ears, whiskers or a muzzle. That is a convolutional network, the classic design for images. Try the real photos too, then switch to the three-class model to see what a “neither” option changes.

Chapter 03 · Image classification · real handwriting

Handwritten digits

Real handwritten digits from a public dataset, reduced to 8 × 8 blocks of ink. Draw your own digit and watch 16 hidden neurons, each a learned stroke template, vote on ten possible answers.

Chapter 04 · Regression · numbers in, a price out

House valuation

The same building blocks as credit scoring with a different ending: one output neuron with no squashing function, trained to minimise squared error. The network outputs a number rather than a class. That is regression.

Chapter 05 · Language model · words in, next-word probabilities out

Predicting the next word

A language model is a classifier whose classes are words. This tiny transformer, the same architecture behind large language models, reads the text so far and gives each of its 167 words a probability of coming next.

Chapter 06 · Generation · the language model in a loop

Completing a sentence

Writing is next-word prediction on repeat: choose a word, append it, run the network again on the longer text. Watch the chapter 05 model finish a sentence, and see where it looks at each step.

Side by side

What changed,
and what didn't.

Every network above does the same thing at its core: multiply by weights, add, squash, and learn by nudging each weight against its gradient. What changes is how the input is turned into numbers, the shape of the network, what the last layer outputs and the loss that defines “wrong”.

Scale

The same maths, far bigger

These networks have 109 to 31,072 parameters. Production image models have millions, and large language models have billions, with sub-word tokens, many more layers and heads, and training on vast amounts of text. The forward pass, the loss, backpropagation and the gradient step are the same ideas.

Honesty

What is real here

Every prediction, probability, attention weight and gradient on this page is computed live from the networks' actual weights. The loans, houses, cat and dog drawings and the language model's sentences are generated by code, so the patterns in them are known and simple. The digits are real handwriting, and the chapter 02 photos are real. The two-class network never trained on photos. The three-class one trained on the photos marked “Training”, and six photos marked “Test” or “Validation” were kept out so it can be tested fairly. Every example on the page is labelled as seen or never seen in training. Applicants and properties are fictional.

Accountability

Decisions about people need more

A real lender must be able to explain a rejection and check that a model does not discriminate, directly or through proxy variables. In the UK and EU, data-protection law gives people safeguards, including human review, for significant decisions made solely by automated means.

Data & code

What each network learned from,
and what it never saw.

Browse or download every example the networks trained on, every example held back to test them, and the notebook with all the training code. To test a network, use held-out examples or your own; examples it trained on only show what it memorised.

A Jupyter notebook with the training code for all six networks, already run so you can read the results, plus the photos, CSV files and a README. About 1 MB.

Marking its own homework

A model tested on its training data is marking its own homework.

A network can score perfectly on examples it trained on simply by memorising them, like a student who has seen the exact exam questions. That is overfitting, and it tells you nothing about new data. So every example is kept in one of three groups, and this page labels each one.

Training

Learned from

Scores here show memory, not skill. The page marks these “seen in training”.

Validation

Used to make choices

Never trained on, but watched while choosing settings such as how long to train, so it slowly stops being neutral.

Test

Locked away

Scored once, after every decision is made. Only this number predicts how the model does on new data.

Where this page had to be careful, and where it slipped
  1. A failed test became training data. The first cat photo was misread by the three-class model, so it was added to its training set. That fixes the symptom and destroys the test, so the photo now sits under “Training photos”, and new photos were brought in for testing.
  2. Validation is not test. The four non-pet photos under “Never used in training” were watched across several training runs while choosing settings. Only the two pets added last are a true test, scored once after training was frozen.
  3. Digits: a choice made on the test set. Network sizes 12, 16 and 24 were compared on the test digits and 16 was kept, so the 97.1% is slightly optimistic. The notebook shows the clean method, choosing on a validation split. The test digits also come from the same 13 writers as the training digits.
  4. Language model: validation copies training. The sentence templates can only produce a few hundred sentences, so 798 of the 800 validation sentences also appear in the training text. The fair probes are the prompts tagged “new combination”.
  5. Credit and house: data that is too clean. Training and validation records come from the same formula. Real lending and property data change over time, so real systems test on a later period than they train on.
  6. Small tests are noisy. Six photos or ten digits cannot pin accuracy down: 3 right out of 6 fits a true accuracy anywhere from 12% to 88%. The page reports these ranges, computed as exact 95% binomial intervals.
